The evaluation covers two teacher/student families—VideoCrafter2/T2V-Turbo-V2 and AnimateDiff/AnimateDiff-Lightning—and includes object, camera, and hybrid motion. This cross-backbone evidence is valuable and supports some generality.

Results show a favorable practical tradeoff. On TurboBench, the 16-step variant improves text alignment, motion fidelity, and FID over the reported baselines in 13 seconds; the 4- and 8-step variants retain competitive motion fidelity with lower latency. Human preferences also consistently favor the proposed method.
The component ablation, hyperparameter studies, extensive qualitative examples, pseudocode, and discussion of misuse and provenance safeguards improve clarity and transparency.
weaknesses: The central mathematical derivation is inconsistent. With the stated loss l=||z_student-z_teacher||^2, subtracting lambda times its gradient yields (1-2lambda)z_student+2lambda z_teacher, not the claimed (1-lambda)z_student+lambda z_teacher. A factor of 1/2 is missing or the update is incorrectly derived. Several teacher updates and timestep intervals are also underspecified or notationally invalid, and Algorithm 1 appears not to break after its early-termination condition. These issues weaken technical confidence and reproducibility.

The adaptive-acceleration evidence is insufficiently controlled. The ablation compares fixed teacher guidance at 20 seconds with the adaptive method at 13 seconds, but the adaptive version unexpectedly improves every quality metric as well as speed. There are no repeated trials, variances, matched-compute comparisons, or separate ablations of activation and dynamic truncation. Consequently, it is unclear whether the gains arise from the policy or sampling variance.

Evaluation sets are small: TurboBench contains only 22 source videos/66 pairs, while AnimateBench contains 15 videos. The paper reports neither multi-seed uncertainty nor statistical significance. The user study likewise omits confidence intervals, randomization/blinding details, and participant-level analysis.

The FID protocol is questionable: it compares generated frames against a reference-image set selected from source videos even though generation uses new text and content. This can reward preservation of source appearance rather than target-video quality, and the very small, insufficiently specified sample set makes FID unreliable. Moreover, FID is attributed to reference [57], which is not the original FID work.

Baseline fairness is difficult to establish because methods use different generators and training regimes. The main method also invokes a large iterative teacher during inference, so describing it as preserving distilled-model efficiency needs qualification: the 16-step system takes 13 seconds versus 4 seconds for the unguided distilled model. No compute counts, memory usage, teacher-call statistics, or quality-versus-compute curves are supplied.

Important implementation details are missing, including image resolution, frame count, window size W, maximum teacher steps, guidance schedule ratio, exact per-motion thresholds, and evaluation sampling protocol. Thresholds are selected from ranges according to motion type without explaining whether this requires manual or oracle knowledge. The supplement also says k=0.01 is used in experiments while later tables favor different k values for object/hybrid motion. Code is only promised, and the project-page field is blank. Overall, the idea and empirical trends are promising, but the mathematical and evaluation uncertainties make the current scientific case slightly short of acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: reference-motion customization is poorly served by few-step distilled video generators, and improving this without model training could be useful.

The teacher-guided refinement is intuitive and reasonably motivated by the mismatch between coarse student trajectories and fine-grained diffusion sampling. The adaptive activation and truncation mechanisms offer a plausible quality-efficiency trade-off.

Evaluation covers two teacher-student model families—VideoCrafter2/T2V-Turbo-V2 and AnimateDiff/AnimateDiff-Lightning—and includes object, camera, and hybrid motion. Compatibility with both MotionClone and MotionDirector provides some evidence of modularity.

The reported improvements are substantial on the selected benchmarks, particularly over directly applying MotionClone to distilled models. Component ablations, multiple sampling budgets, qualitative examples, and a 50-participant user study provide several complementary forms of evidence.
The presentation is generally organized, and the supplement includes pseudocode, further qualitative comparisons, hyperparameter studies, and a meaningful discussion of misuse and provenance risks.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is not sufficiently controlled to support the broad state-of-the-art claims. Comparisons mix different backbones, initialization schemes, training regimes, and sampling budgets. A matched teacher-only baseline using exactly the same initialization, motion loss, schedule, and compute budget is missing, making it difficult to isolate the benefit of the proposed student-teacher formulation.

The evaluation sets are very small and partly nonstandard: TurboBench contains only 22 unique videos, while AnimateBench contains 15. Videos are drawn partly from unspecified online sources, and prompts, splits, selection criteria, and source URLs are not provided. There are no confidence intervals, per-category results, repeated-seed analyses, or statistical tests, so the robustness of modest metric differences is unclear.

The FID protocol is questionable. FID is computed against frames from selected source videos even though customization intentionally changes subject and scene appearance; this can reward source-appearance leakage rather than output realism. The sample count and feature-extraction details are also omitted. Moreover, the FID citation is misattributed, and the supplement incorrectly cites that reference as ControlVideo, raising attribution and quality-control concerns.

For a video-motion paper, the manuscript supplies only frame strips and an empty project-page field rather than accessible video results. Static frames cannot adequately demonstrate motion fidelity, temporal artifacts, or camera trajectories, substantially limiting verification of the central claims.

Reproducibility is poor for the central adaptive strategy. Essential values or protocols for W, Nmax, tau, t_alpha, teacher starting step, guidance scales, and motion-type-dependent threshold selection are missing or incomplete. The authors state that thresholds vary according to motion type but do not explain how the type is determined at test time, suggesting manual or oracle tuning. Grid search is apparently performed on the same small evaluation benchmarks without a validation split.

The central adaptive components are not separately evaluated. Only the complete adaptive strategy is added in Table 3; there is no isolation of step-wise activation versus dynamic truncation, no sensitivity analysis for delta_1 or delta_2, and no report of how often guidance activates or how many teacher evaluations are saved. Consequently, the claimed mechanism behind the efficiency gain remains unverified.

The formulation called “test-time distillation” is essentially convex interpolation between student and teacher clean-latent predictions. The equality between the stated gradient update and Eq. (5) requires an unstated absorption of the squared-loss gradient factor into lambda. More broadly, the paper provides little analysis of why this interpolation is preferable to ordinary teacher-guided sampling.

Algorithm 1 contains ambiguities that impede implementation: initialization of the moving-loss window is unspecified, dynamic truncation updates the interval endpoint without an explicit break, subsequent loop state can therefore be undefined, and fresh random noise is repeatedly introduced without clarifying coupling or reproducibility. The prose and equations also inconsistently describe timestep interval direction and endpoints.

The efficiency claim needs stronger accounting. Runtime depends heavily on resolution, video length, software, inversion, attention-gradient computation, and triggered teacher steps, but these details and variance are absent. On AnimateDiff, the proposed eight-step method takes 24 seconds versus seven seconds for direct MC+AD-L, so the characterization as preserving the efficiency of distilled generation is only partially supported.

The user study lacks key protocol details such as randomization, blinding, presentation order, whether videos could be replayed, participant-level aggregation, and uncertainty estimates. The supplied screenshots do not establish that temporal behavior was presented adequately, so the study cannot fully compensate for weaknesses in the automatic metrics.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important gap: existing training-free motion-customization techniques degrade substantially when applied to few-step distilled video generators. Framing teacher assistance as adaptive test-time distillation is intuitive and relevant to efficient video generation.

The method is technically coherent overall. Reference-aware initialization, teacher-guided endpoint interpolation, step-wise guidance activation, and dynamic truncation form a sensible pipeline for reconciling fine-grained teacher trajectories with coarse student sampling.

The empirical results are consistently favorable. On TurboBench, the 16-step method improves motion fidelity from 0.876 to 0.933 and FID from 369.49 to 322.97 over MotionClone while reducing reported inference time from 114 s to 13 s. The 8- and 4-step variants retain competitive quality, demonstrating a useful quality-efficiency trade-off.

Evaluation covers two distinct distilled-model families, T2V-Turbo-V2/VideoCrafter2 and AnimateDiff-Lightning/AnimateDiff, as well as object, camera, and hybrid motion. This provides meaningful evidence that the framework is not tied to one particular student-teacher pair.

The component-wise ablation is informative: motion guidance, inverted-reference initialization, teacher guidance, and adaptive acceleration each produce measurable effects. In particular, adaptive acceleration reduces inference from 20 s to 13 s while improving the reported aggregate metrics.

The extensive qualitative results and 50-participant user study broadly agree with the automatic metrics. The paper is well organized, includes implementation thresholds and pseudocode, and discusses limitations and potential misuse.
weaknesses: The evaluation benchmarks are small and partly assembled from selected or online videos: TurboBench contains 66 prompt-video pairs from 22 videos, while AnimateBench contains only 15 videos. There are no confidence intervals, repeated-seed results, or significance tests, so robustness of the relatively small metric differences is uncertain.

The FID protocol is questionable for this task. It compares generated frames with images selected from source videos even though customization intentionally changes the source content, and FID is unreliable on such small sample sets. FVD or distributional video metrics, together with per-category statistics, would provide stronger evidence.

Efficiency comparisons need tighter controls. The paper does not fully specify output resolution and length, whether inversion and preprocessing are included uniformly, or the exact sampling configurations used by every baseline. MotionEcho also requires simultaneous access to a large teacher, so its memory cost and the distinction between latency and total computation should be reported.

Several mathematical and algorithmic details are imprecise. For the stated squared distillation loss, a gradient step gives a factor of two and does not directly equal the claimed convex interpolation unless the loss contains a one-half factor or the step size is redefined. Algorithm 1 also lacks an explicit break after dynamic truncation, leaves moving-window boundary handling unspecified, and uses fresh renoising noise without explaining whether noise is shared across teacher and student paths.

The adaptive thresholds vary by motion type, but the paper does not explain how the motion type or threshold is selected for a new input. Sensitivity is shown for several other hyperparameters but not for the central activation and truncation thresholds, which weakens the claimed adaptivity and reproducibility.

The main comparison mixes training-based and training-free methods with different architectures and operating points. Stronger controlled comparisons against fixed-step teacher guidance, uniformly reduced teacher steps, and equal-compute baselines would better establish that the proposed adaptive policy itself—not simply additional teacher computation—causes the gains.

The user-study reporting omits randomization and blinding details, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty estimates, and a clear explanation of whether participants selected one winner or could assign ties. These omissions make the preference margins difficult to interpret statistically.

MotionEcho offers a simple, broadly applicable solution: selectively run a compatible teacher within student intervals, form a motion-corrected clean endpoint, and interpolate it with the student's endpoint. The approach requires no parameter training and can reuse multiple motion objectives.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. Results cover UNet- and DiT-based generators, several distilled families (TurboV2, Video-Blade, AnimateDiff-Lightning, TDM, and Wan2.2 variants), three motion-guidance methods, multiple motion types, and an additional public benchmark.

The central empirical case is convincing: on TurboBench, teacher guidance raises motion fidelity from 0.833 to 0.912, while adaptive scheduling further raises it to 0.933 and reduces runtime from 20 s to 13 s. Direct student-only comparisons on Video-Blade also show large motion-fidelity gains, mitigating the concern that improvements arise only from changing backbones.

The paper reports useful efficiency information, including inference time and peak memory. Although MotionEcho is slower than uncorrected students, it remains much faster than dense teacher-based guidance, and the quality-efficiency trade-off is practically meaningful.

The presentation is generally clear, with pseudocode, hyperparameters, component and sensitivity ablations, qualitative examples, a disclosed failure case, and a substantive discussion of limitations and misuse risks.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate. The core correction is a convex interpolation between student and teacher clean predictions; presenting it as score-distillation optimization does not provide a substantive theoretical guarantee. The claim that direct optimization through the student is "fundamentally intractable" is overstated: it is expensive, but ordinary differentiation through diffusion networks is routinely performed.

The adaptive mechanism is less automatic than suggested. TurboV2 uses manually selected motion-type-specific guidance strengths, noise blending factors, and activation/truncation thresholds. This apparently requires knowing whether each example contains camera, object, or hybrid motion, and no automatic categorization procedure or cross-dataset threshold-transfer experiment is supplied.

There is a reproducibility inconsistency around Nmax. The appendix describes it as the maximum number of teacher-distillation events per sample, whereas Algorithm 1 uses it to terminate the teacher's inner denoising loop and contains no counter that limits the number of activated events. The choice of the intermediate teacher timestep s is also left unspecified.

Most evaluation relies on small, author-assembled benchmarks: TurboBench has 22 source videos and DavisBench has 34. The paper reports only point estimates, without repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly limiting for stochastic generation and for several fairly small metric differences.

Some comparisons are confounded by different backbones, resolutions, control signals, and optimization procedures. The student-only comparisons in Table 10 are valuable, but equivalent controlled comparisons are not consistently provided for every backbone and baseline. Runtime is reported only on one GPU, without detailed accounting of inversion, feature extraction, and optimization costs for each method.

The FID protocol is questionable: it compares generated frames against a small image set derived from source videos, although the target prompts intentionally change appearance and semantics. This score can reward source-appearance leakage and is statistically unreliable at the reported benchmark sizes. A video-quality metric and distributionally appropriate target set would make the quality claim stronger.

The user study lacks essential procedural and statistical details, including assignment counts per participant, presentation-order randomization, blinding, treatment of ties, inter-rater agreement, and confidence intervals. Consequently, the reported win-rate margins are difficult to interpret.

The method still requires a compatible high-quality teacher with a shared latent space and increases cost substantially over the distilled model alone (for example, 7 s to 13 s and 27 GB to 36 GB on TurboV2). Thus, claims that it preserves distilled-generation efficiency should be phrased as retaining a favorable trade-off rather than preserving the original efficiency.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically relevant problem: motion-guidance methods designed for dense diffusion trajectories can degrade substantially when directly applied to few-step distilled video generators.

MotionEcho is conceptually simple and modular. Correcting a student's predicted clean endpoint using selective teacher-generated endpoints can be combined with several motion objectives, including MotionClone, MOFT, DMT, and DiTFlow.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering UNet- and DiT-based students derived from VideoCrafter2, AnimateDiff, Wan2.1/Wan2.2, and CogVideoX. The supplementary material also reports memory, runtime, additional metrics, a failure case, and ethical considerations.

Same-student comparisons provide some evidence for the core idea. For example, on TurboV2, adding teacher guidance raises MF from 0.833 to 0.912, and on Video-Blade the proposed variants substantially improve MF over directly applying the corresponding guidance method.

The paper is generally organized around a clear motivation, method, and evaluation, and it explicitly acknowledges difficulty with fine-grained motion and large source-target structural discrepancies.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty is limited. The purported test-time distillation update reduces to a heuristic convex interpolation between student and teacher clean predictions. Treating the clean prediction as an independent variable avoids the Jacobian only by replacing the original optimization problem; the paper provides no analysis showing that this surrogate restores the intended trajectory or improves stability. The derivation largely restates the interpolation algebraically.

The central efficiency evidence is not trustworthy as currently documented. TurboV2 experiments require 200-step DDIM inversion of every reference video, yet the method is reported as taking only 13 seconds and ITC is described as the total time required for motion transfer. It is unclear whether inversion, reference-feature extraction, teacher loading, and other preprocessing are excluded or amortized. Since efficiency is a primary claim, complete end-to-end timings and a precise accounting protocol are necessary.

Many headline comparisons are not controlled. Table 1 compares methods using ControlNet or full VideoCrafter2 against MotionEcho using TurboV2, while Table 2 compares full Wan2.1 baselines against a Video-Blade student. Backbone, resolution, frame count, sampling schedule, optimization budget, and implementation quality can therefore explain part of the reported quality and speed differences. The more informative matched-student results are relegated to ablations and do not cover all claims.

The evaluation metrics are problematic. FID is computed against frames from selected source videos even though target prompts intentionally alter appearance, so lower FID may reward retaining source content rather than generating the requested target. CLIP similarity between adjacent frames is also a weak temporal-quality measure and can reward static videos. Although MF and Flow-sim help, no confidence intervals, repeated-seed results, or statistical tests are reported despite small and correlated custom test sets.

The adaptive strategy is insufficiently validated. There is no matched-compute comparison against a fixed teacher schedule, and the full adaptive variant is simultaneously faster and better than uniform teacher guidance without an analysis of teacher-call frequency or why selection improves quality. Thresholds are motion-type- and backbone-specific, weakening claims that the method requires little tuning.

There are reproducibility inconsistencies. The supplement defines Nmax as the maximum number of teacher-distillation events per sample, whereas Algorithm 1 uses it to cap inner teacher denoising steps. The pseudocode also appears not to break after its truncation condition. Online benchmark videos and complete prompt/source specifications are not provided, and code is only promised after acceptance.

The user study is under-specified: it does not report assignment counts per example, presentation randomization, ties, quality control, inter-rater agreement, or uncertainty. Static frame strips in the PDF cannot independently substantiate claims about motion fidelity and temporal coherence, and the manuscript provides no accessible project/video link.

Several claims are overstated. The approach does not preserve the original distilled model's efficiency: it increases TurboV2 runtime from 7 to 13 seconds and Video-Blade runtime from roughly 32–34 to 49–54 seconds, while requiring both teacher and student models and up to 36 GB of memory. It is faster than full-teacher guidance, but that narrower trade-off should replace claims of retaining efficiency without compromise.

Assessed as Algorithms/General because no contribution type is explicitly declared. Under that standard, the practical idea and broad experiments are merits, but limited algorithmic novelty, unclear end-to-end cost, and insufficiently controlled evidence leave the principal effectiveness-and-efficiency case unconvincing. These are substantive issues rather than presentation-only corrections.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important failure mode: motion-guidance techniques designed for dense diffusion trajectories degrade substantially on few-step distilled video generators. The motivating comparisons make this problem concrete.

MotionEcho offers a simple, coherent solution: use the distilled student as the main generator, selectively construct a motion-corrected endpoint with the teacher, and interpolate the teacher and student clean predictions. The adaptive activation and truncation mechanisms address the central efficiency–fidelity trade-off.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad. Results cover UNet- and DiT-based generators, several distillation paradigms and model scales, multiple motion-guidance methods, and additional backbones including AnimateDiff-Lightning, Video-Blade, TDM, and Wan2.2 variants.

The improvements in motion fidelity are substantial and consistent. For example, on the VB setting, MotionEcho raises MF from 0.491–0.567 to approximately 0.731–0.733, while the TurboV2 ablation raises MF from 0.833 with motion guidance alone to 0.933 with the complete method.

The component ablation, hyperparameter studies, per-motion-type evaluation, optical-flow metric, user study, memory analysis, and disclosed failure case collectively provide credible evidence beyond a single benchmark number. The paper is also clearly organized and includes useful pseudocode, implementation settings, limitations, and societal-impact discussion.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, this is a practically meaningful contribution whose value comes from diagnosing and repairing an emerging compatibility problem rather than from introducing a fundamentally new generative architecture.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. Once a compatible teacher is available, the central update is a convex interpolation of teacher and student endpoint predictions, while the adaptive policy consists of thresholding motion loss. Calling this score distillation somewhat overstates the technical depth, and the claim that differentiation through the student is “fundamentally intractable” should instead be framed as computationally expensive.

Some headline comparisons confound the proposed method with different backbones. Table 1 compares the TurboV2-based method against several VideoCrafter2 or ControlNet systems, and Table 2 compares a VB student against full Wan2.1 baselines. The supplementary same-backbone VB comparison helps considerably, but similarly controlled comparisons should be foregrounded for every major setting.

The adaptive scheduler is not compared against fixed or random teacher schedules under matched teacher-call and runtime budgets. Consequently, Table 3 establishes that selective guidance is faster than uniform guidance, but does not fully show that the proposed loss-based activation rule is better than simpler compute-matched scheduling.

The method remains dependent on a compatible, high-quality teacher at inference time and generally assumes shared or compatible latent spaces. Relative to the distilled baseline, runtime increases from 7 to 13 seconds on TurboV2 and roughly 32–34 to 49–54 seconds on VB, with TurboV2 memory rising from 27 to 36 GB. Thus, claims about preserving distilled efficiency should be qualified as retaining an advantage over full-teacher customization rather than retaining the original student cost.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates across seeds or confidence intervals. The user study also omits important protocol details such as the number of ratings per participant and case, presentation randomization, quality control, inter-rater agreement, and statistical significance.

Reproducibility details contain an apparent inconsistency: the supplement describes Nmax as the maximum number of teacher-distillation events per sample, whereas Algorithm 1 uses it as a bound on inner teacher denoising steps and does not visibly count sample-level activation events. Motion-type-specific thresholds and blend factors also appear to require knowing whether a test case is object, camera, or hybrid motion.

Metric and dataset construction deserve more scrutiny. FID against source-video frames is difficult to interpret when the target prompt intentionally changes appearance, and the main benchmarks are modest in size. The inclusion of online videos also needs exact source, license, prompt, and split documentation. Finally, the FID citation appears incorrectly attributed rather than citing the standard Heusel et al. work.
